doc.title: Chazz Frichtel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 13, 2016

title: The Dangling Carrot and an aging music business
summary: His book title idea, and how the business has changed and he is now old guard.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: We’ll lighten it up a little bit. The other day when we were chatting I heard the term “dangling carrot.”

Oh man, the dangling carrot. Well we were talking about — my partner Carolyn keeps telling me I should write a book. And about as far as I’ve gotten on the book is coming up with the title which I thought was The Dangling Carrot which is kind of funny because sometimes in the music business it seems like you’re just about there, you’re just about there and you’re going to snap down on this carrot, whatever the carrot might be, and oops, it’s over there. But fortunately for me I got to take a few chunks out of the carrot. So I’m grateful and really happy about that. But as you know, and as everybody who’s ever been in the business know, it’s a challenging way to make a living. Because you never know, you’re only as good as your last gig. You never know if you’re going to get the next call or when it’s going to come. You’re hopeful, and I was lucky enough to where I had a nice ride. And I’m still active in the music business but the business has changed and it’s very different than it was even ten years ago. And I hate to say it as someone who’s played in a lot of pop formats, I’m 63 now and that format is a whole new generation coming up. And I have to consider myself part of the old guard and we’re kind of moving to the side, whether we want to or not. And believe me, a lot of the old guard doesn’t want to go, they’re going down kicking and fighting you know.
